blocks.content: Constitutional status provides institutional permanence, safeguarding democratic bodies from political whims and ensuring uniform implementation across all states.

rows: Mentioned directly in the Constitution of India
Created by an Act of Parliament or State Legislature
Requires a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368
Can be modified or repealed by passing an ordinary law
Election Commission, UPSC, CAG, Finance Commission
NHRC, SEBI, National Green Tribunal (NGT), UIDAI

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Constitutional bodies derive their powers, duties, and authority directly from specific articles of the Constitution of India.
The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts of 1992 conferred constitutional status on rural and urban local self-governments.
Conferring constitutional status ensures institutional permanence, protecting bodies from being dissolved by ordinary legislative action.
Major constitutional bodies include the Election Commission (Article 324), Comptroller and Auditor General (Article 148), UPSC (Article 315), and Finance Commission (Article 280).
Any modification to the powers or structure of constitutional bodies typically requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
Distinction between Constitutional bodies (e.g., CAG, UPSC) and Statutory/Non-Constitutional bodies (e.g., NITI Aayog, NHRC) is a frequently asked topic.
Remember key constitutional articles: Article 324 (Election Commission), Article 280 (Finance Commission), and Article 148 (CAG).
The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act came into force on April 24, 1993, which is celebrated annually as National Panchayati Raj Day.
